records.title: openrisc: Add text patching API support
records.body:
Add text patching api's to use in subsequent jump_label implementation.  We use
a new fixmap FIX_TEXT_POKE0 entry to temporarily override MMU mappings to allow
read only text pages to be written to.

Previously, __set_fix was marked with __init as it was only used during the
EARLYCON stage. Now that TEXT_POKE mappings require post-init usage
(e.g., FIX_TEXT_POKE0), keeping __init would cause runtime bugs whenset_fixmap
accesses invalid memory. Thus, we remove the __init flag to ensure __set_fix
remains valid beyond initialization.

A new function patch_insn_write is exposed to allow single instruction patching.

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/openrisc/aJIC8o1WmVHol9RY@antec/T/#t

Signed-off-by: chenmiao <chenmiao.ku@gmail.com>

RV64 version and add the CONFIG_JUMP_LABEL=y to the defconfig.

+/*

+ * Based on arch/arm/include/asm/jump_label.h

+#ifndef __ASM_OPENRISC_JUMP_LABEL_H
+#define __ASM_OPENRISC_JUMP_LABEL_H
+
+#ifndef __ASSEMBLER__
+
+#include <linux/types.h>
+#include <asm/insn-def.h>
+
+#define HAVE_JUMP_LABEL_BATCH
+
+#define JUMP_LABEL_NOP_SIZE OPENRISC_INSN_SIZE

+/**
+ * JUMP_TABLE_ENTRY - Create a jump table entry
+ * @key: Jump key identifier (typically a symbol address)
+ * @label: Target label address
+ *
+ * This macro creates a jump table entry in the dedicated kernel section (__jump_table).
+ * Each entry contains the following information:
+ * 		Offset from current instruction to jump instruction (1b - .)
+ * 		Offset from current instruction to target label (label - .)
+ * 		Offset from current instruction to key identifier (key - .)
+ */
+#define JUMP_TABLE_ENTRY(key, label)			\
+	".pushsection	__jump_table, \"aw\"	\n\t"	\
+	".align 	4 			\n\t"	\
+	".long 		1b - ., " label " - .	\n\t"	\
+	".long 		" key " - . 		\n\t"	\
+	".popsection				\n\t"
+
+#define ARCH_STATIC_BRANCH_ASM(key, label)		\
+	".align		4			\n\t"	\
+	"1: l.nop				\n\t"	\
+	"    l.nop				\n\t"	\
+	JUMP_TABLE_ENTRY(key, label)
+
+static __always_inline bool arch_static_branch(struct static_key *const key,
+					       const bool branch)
+{
+	asm goto (ARCH_STATIC_BRANCH_ASM("%0", "%l[l_yes]")
+		  ::"i"(&((char *)key)[branch])::l_yes);
+
+	return false;
+l_yes:
+	return true;
+}
+

+	".align		4			\n\t"	\
+	"1: l.j	" label "			\n\t"	\
+	"    l.nop				\n\t"	\
+	JUMP_TABLE_ENTRY(key, label)
+
+static __always_inline bool
+arch_static_branch_jump(struct static_key *const key, const bool branch)
+{
+	asm goto (ARCH_STATIC_BRANCH_JUMP_ASM("%0", "%l[l_yes]")
+		  ::"i"(&((char *)key)[branch])::l_yes);
+
+	return false;
+l_yes:
+	return true;
+}
+
+#endif /* __ASSEMBLER__ */
+#endif /* __ASM_OPENRISC_JUMP_LABEL_H */

While working on #<!-- -->225037, where using an enum as the element type of `ext_vector_type` triggers an assertion failure, we added regression tests covering template instantiation in PR #<!-- -->228863 and discovered an additional diagnostic location issue. This issue also reproduces without the changes from PR #<!-- -->228863, using a struct as the element type.

For the test case below, instantiating `Vector<S>` correctly produces an error about the invalid element type. struct S {};

``` txt
      |           ^
1 error generated.
```

Expected behavior:

The primary error diagnostic should include a valid source location pointing to the relevant `ext_vector_type` attribute in the template, while preserving the existing template instantiation note.

Related discussion: https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/pull/228863#discussion_r4188767251
</details>

records.title: [libc][stdlib] Avoid scanning values during environment lookup
records.body:
Constructing a string_view for each environment entry scans the entire value to determine its length, even when the name does not match. This makes lookups unnecessarily expensive for long values such as PATH.

Filter entries by their first character, then compare the remaining name up to a mismatch or null terminator. Require a following '=' to match the complete key, preserving support for empty names in putenv.

Closes #196016

records.title: [libc] Request for Annex K via `__STDC_WANT_LIB_EXT1__` doesn't work as expected
records.body:
Source code:
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#define __STDC_WANT_LIB_EXT1__ 1
#include <string.h>

int foo() {
  return strnlen_s("abc", 2);
}
```
Compile with:
`clang -c a.c`

We get the error:
```
a.c:6:10: error: call to undeclared function 'strnlen_s'; ISO C99 and later do not support implicit function declarations [-Wimplicit-function-declaration]
    6 |   return strnlen_s("abc", 2);
      |          ^
```

If we move the line `#define __STDC_WANT_LIB_EXT1__ 1` before `#include <stdio.h>`, it works as expected.

**Analysis**

I believe this issue is caused by the header inclusion guard in `llvm-libc-macros/annex-k-macros.h`.

The inclusion of `stdio.h` implies a recursive inclusion of `annex-k-macros.h`. But at that point, the `__STDC_WANT_LIB_EXT1__` is not yet defined, therefore the macro who controls the availability of Annex K functionality, `LIBC_HAS_ANNEX_K`, is not defined.

By the time `__STDC_WANT_LIB_EXT1__` is defined and `string.h` is included, the recursive inclusion of `annex-k-macros.h` (by the second time now) is stopped at the header inclusion guard, hence `LIBC_HAS_ANNEX_K` is again not defined. As a result, the declaration of `strnlen_s` is never brought in.

Found by @simpal01

I reproduced the issue locally. While working on a fix, I put together the following test:

1. https://godbolt.org/z/nYY41P38G
2. https://godbolt.org/z/GcoKK7Eqs
3. https://godbolt.org/z/heW44dPY3

``` cc
extern "C" void* resolver() {
  return nullptr;
}

[[gnu::weak, gnu::ifunc("resolver")]] void selector();  // first, GCC error, Clang ok

void selector(void) __attribute__((ifunc("resolver"))); // second, GCC ok, Clang ok

[[gnu::ifunc("resolver")]]void selector(void); // third, GCC ok, Clang ok

#pragma weak selector

```

Of the three cases, **GCC diagnoses the first but accepts the second and third, while Clang accepts all three**.

I compiled each of the three test cases separately on my local machine and inspected the resulting object-file symbols. The results are as follows:

``` text
OS: Fedora Linux 44
Clang: clang version 22.1.8 (Fedora 22.1.8-4.fc44)
GCC: gcc version 16.2.1 20260819 (Red Hat 16.2.1-2)
```

| Test case | Clang | GCC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| first | Strong IFUNC; weak is not preserved | Error; no object file produced |
| second | Strong IFUNC | Weak IFUNC |
| third| Strong IFUNC | Weak IFUNC |

In the versions and configuration I tested, Clang silently ignores weak in all three cases, whereas GCC rejects the explicit combination but emits a **`weak IFUNC`** in the two cases using `#pragma weak`.

As far as I understand, `ISO C/C++` does not specify how weak and ifunc should interact. **However, the [GCC documentation](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-15.2.0/gcc/Common-Function-Attributes.html#index-ifunc-function-attribute) states that “Indirect functions cannot be weak,” and the [Clang documentation](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AttributeReference.html#ifunc) states that “The entity must not have weak linkage.”**

Based on these documented restrictions, should the second and third cases also be rejected? In other words, **is the restriction on the resulting entity’s linkage, regardless of how it is specified?** If so, an `IFUNC` with `weak` linkage should be rejected even when the attributes are introduced through separate declarations or the weak linkage is introduced via `#pragma weak`.

records.title: [clang] Fix crash on unterminated __identifier
records.body:
With Microsoft extensions enabled, e.g. via `-fms-compatibility`, the following input triggers an assertion:

```cpp
# 1 __identifier(foo
```

The `__identifier` handler consumes the end-of-directive token, `eod`, while looking for `)`, but still returns `foo` to the line-marker handler. The latter rejects `foo` as an invalid filename and tries to discard the remaining tokens up to the end of the directive. Since `eod` has already been consumed, it encounters `eof` and triggers an assertion.

Return `eod`, `eof`, and `annotation` tokens to the caller when recovering from a missing `)`.

Fixes #222310

records.title: [clang][Sema] Avoid out-of-bounds format_arg access
records.body:
Clang implicitly adds `format_arg(1)` to `__CFStringMakeConstantString`, including declarations created during error recovery. A zero-argument call can therefore make `checkFormatStringExpr` access a nonexistent argument.

Reproducer:

```c
void a(char *) __attribute__((format(__CFString__, 1, 2)));
void b() { a(__CFStringMakeConstantString()); }
```

Before this change, an assertions-enabled build crashes after reporting the source errors (diagnostic excerpts):

```text
error: call to undeclared function '__CFStringMakeConstantString';
       ISO C99 and later do not support implicit function declarations
error: incompatible integer to pointer conversion passing 'int' to parameter of type 'char *'
Assertion `Arg < getNumArgs() && "Arg access out of range!"' failed.
```

Check the `format_arg` index against `CE->getNumArgs()` before calling `CE->getArg()`. Return `SLCT_NotALiteral` when the argument is missing so normal diagnostics can continue.

After this change, the compiler reports diagnostics and exits with status 1 without crashing (diagnostic excerpts):

```text
error: call to undeclared function '__CFStringMakeConstantString';
       ISO C99 and later do not support implicit function declarations
error: incompatible integer to pointer conversion passing 'int' to parameter of type 'char *'
warning: format string is not a string literal (potentially insecure)
```

Fixes #225034

records.title: [clang] Fix pragma attribute crashes caused by nested _Pragma
records.body:
A nested `_Pragma` can produce an `annot_pragma_attribute` token during preprocessing. After diagnosing invalid attribute syntax, `HandlePragmaAttribute` calls `getIdentifierInfo()` to generate a fix-it without checking whether the current token is an annotation. `getAttributeSubjectRulesRecoveryPointForToken`, which handles recovery for attribute subject rules, has the same problem.

For example, this input enters the attribute syntax error path:

```c
#pragma clang attribute (_Pragma("clang attribute push"))
```

In the following input, the attribute itself is valid, but a nested `_Pragma` appears where `apply_to` is expected, entering the attribute subject rule recovery path:

```c
#pragma clang attribute push(__attribute__((annotate("test"))), _Pragma("clang attribute push"))
```

Before this change, both inputs fail in assertion-enabled builds with:

```text
Assertion `!isAnnotation() && "getIdentifierInfo() on an annotation token!"' failed.
```

Check for annotation tokens before querying identifier information in `HandlePragmaAttribute`. Return `None` for annotation tokens in `getAttributeSubjectRulesRecoveryPointForToken` so that the existing error recovery logic can handle them.

The two inputs now produce the following diagnostics, respectively:

```text
error: expected an attribute that is specified using the GNU, C++11 or '__declspec' syntax
error: expected attribute subject set specifier 'apply_to'
```

Fixes #225035

records.title: [clang][Sema] Check swift_attr argument count in type contexts
records.body:
`HandleSwiftAttr` checks the first argument with
`checkStringLiteralArgumentAttr` without validating the argument count. Unlike declaration attributes, this path does not go through `checkCommonAttributeFeatures`, so a missing argument causes an out-of-bounds access in `ParsedAttr::getArg`.

For example:

```c
int * __attribute__((__swift_attr__)) a;
```

Before this change, compiling this code crashes. In assertion-enabled builds, it fails in `ParsedAttr::getArg` with:

```text
Assertion `Arg < NumArgs && "Arg access out of range!"' failed.
```

Check that the attribute has exactly one argument in `HandleSwiftAttr` before reading it so that the same code produces a diagnostic instead:

```text
error: '__swift_attr__' attribute takes one argument
```

Fixes #227549

records.title: [libc][math] Prevent spurious floating-point exceptions in fdim
records.body:
Without `FENV_ACCESS` enabled, Clang at `-O2` optimizes the conditional expression in `fdim`:

```cpp
return x > y ? x - y : T(0);
```

into the following LLVM IR:

```llvm
%cmp = fcmp ogt double %x, %y
%diff = fsub double %x, %y
%result = select i1 %cmp, double %diff, double 0.000000e+00
```

The `fsub` is not guarded by `x > y`. Even when `x <= y`, the subtraction executes before `select` chooses zero as the result. The `select` only chooses a value; it cannot undo floating-point exceptions already raised by the subtraction. Consequently, `fdim(-inf, -inf)` raises `FE_INVALID`, `fdim(-max, -min_subnormal)` raises `FE_INEXACT`, and `fdim(-max, max)` can raise `FE_OVERFLOW` and `FE_INEXACT`, despite all these calls returning zero.

Without floating-point environment access enabled, the compiler need not preserve the observable behavior of these exceptions and can speculate the subtraction. Simply rewriting the conditional expression as an `if` statement does not reliably prevent this optimization.

Enable `FENV_ACCESS` in the shared implementation so the subtraction uses `llvm.experimental.constrained.fsub` with dynamic rounding and strict exception semantics. The optimized IR keeps the subtraction in the `x > y` branch, avoiding spurious exceptions on the path that returns zero. Enable `FENV_ACCESS` in the public entry points as well to allow the strict floating-point implementation to be inlined.

Fixes #88771

comments.body:
@epage @AlexTMjugador I think `build.warnings` should have consistent semantics across human-readable and JSON output. `--message-format` should only change how messages are represented, not how warnings are handled.

Specifically, I would lean toward:
- `allow`: Filter out lint warning diagnostics, including the corresponding JSON messages, without failing the build or emitting an additional notice.
- `warn` (the default): Preserve lint warning diagnostics without failing the build because of them.
- `deny`: Preserve lint warning diagnostics, but fail the build and explain why, without changing the original diagnostics to `error`.

As for `-D warnings`, my understanding is that it promotes the relevant lint diagnostics to errors within Clippy, so they would remain visible even with `build.warnings = "allow"`. Downstream tools could still consume those errors, for example to generate SARIF. This would, however, filter out diagnostics that remain at the warning level when `allow` is set, which I think is consistent with the user explicitly choosing to suppress lint warnings.

comments.author: AlexTMjugador
comments.body: My two cents on the design questions: for my use case of converting Clippy output to SARIF, it's quite useful to preserve whatever lints Clippy outputs as-is, mirroring the traditional `-D` switch behavior. More generally, I can imagine the chief use case of `--message-format=json` to get structured, machine-friendly output from Clippy that can then be converted into another representation. So whatever is deemed to make that task more ergonomic sounds reasonable to me.

Closes #17519

### What does this PR try to resolve?

Minimal reproduction:

```
fn main() { 
  let unused = 1; 
}

cargo clippy --config 'build.warnings="deny"' --message-format=json
echo $?
```

Expected: exit code 101.
Actual: exit code 0, with `"success": true` in the `build-finished` message.

JSON diagnostics bypass warning accounting. This change counts JSON lint warnings so the existing deny handling applies, while preserving the original compiler failure when errors and warnings occur together.

`cargo clippy --message-format=json` succeeds despite lint warnings when `build.warnings = "deny"` is set, because JSON diagnostics bypass warning accounting.

Count JSON lint warnings so the existing deny handling applies. Preserve the original compiler failure when errors and warnings occur together.

### How to test and review this PR?

Added regression coverage for JSON output formats, cached diagnostics, `--keep-going`, and mixed errors and warnings.

```sh
cargo test -p cargo --test testsuite warning_override
```

All 16 tests pass. Also verified the Clippy reproduction from #17519: it now exits with 101 and emits `"success": false`.

records.title: [clang] Reject enum element types in ext_vector_type (#228863)
records.body:
`BuildExtVectorType` checks element types with `isIntegerType()`, which
also accepts complete unscoped enums. However,
`ASTContext::getExtVectorType` does not support enum elements.

For example:

```c
typedef enum { A } E;
typedef E V __attribute__((ext_vector_type(4)));
```

Before this change, compiling with `-fsyntax-only` in an
assertion-enabled build crashes in `ASTContext::getExtVectorType`:

```text
clang: clang/lib/AST/ASTContext.cpp:4839:
QualType clang::ASTContext::getExtVectorType(QualType, unsigned int) const:
Assertion `vecType->isBuiltinType() || vecType->isDependentType() ||
(vecType->isBitIntType() && llvm::isPowerOf2_32(vecType->castAs<BitIntType>()->getNumBits()))' failed.
```

Explicitly reject enum element types in `BuildExtVectorType` so that the
same code produces a diagnostic instead:

```text
error: invalid vector element type 'E'
```

Fixes #225037
